set.detail:
In 149, after Carthage's war with Masinissa (150), which violated the treaty of 201, Rome declared war. Utica, the second city of Carthaginian Africa, had already surrendered to Rome, giving it a base. Carthaginian envoys came to Rome and surrendered their city by deditio, an act by which they placed themselves entirely in Roman hands. The Senate promised that Carthage would keep its freedom, its laws, its territory and its property, on condition that it sent 300 hostages, children of the leading families, to the consuls in Sicily within 30 days, and obeyed the consuls' further orders.

The consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus crossed with 80,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry (Appian) to Utica. They demanded that Carthage surrender all its weapons; Carthage handed over 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Then Censorinus announced the final demand: the Carthaginians must abandon their city, which would be destroyed, and settle at least 80 stades (about 15 kilometres) from the sea. Appian (Punica 80-89) gives Censorinus' speech, arguing that the sea had corrupted Carthage and that the Senate had promised to preserve the Carthaginian state (civitas), not the city (urbs).

The Carthaginian envoys were horrified; when the demand was reported, the people of Carthage rioted, killed senators who had advised surrender, and killed the Italians in the city. They decided to fight, freed slaves, and worked day and night to make weapons: Appian says they produced 100 shields, 300 swords, 1,000 catapult bolts and 500 javelins a day, and the women cut their hair to make catapult ropes. Polybius (36.2-9) discusses the morality of the Roman behaviour, presenting the arguments of Greek critics who saw it as deceit, and of those who defended its legality. Modern historians see the series of demands as a deliberate policy to destroy Carthage without the risks of a major war, a cynical exploitation of the legal concept of deditio.

scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)
Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth, in Ethics and Rhetoric (1995)

set.detail:
In 149 the tribune Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi carried a law establishing a permanent court (quaestio perpetua) to hear cases of extortion (de pecuniis repetundis) by Roman magistrates in the provinces. The court was presided over by a praetor, with a jury drawn from the Senate. It was a civil procedure for the restitution of money extorted, not a criminal punishment; provincials could bring complaints through a Roman patron.

The background was a series of scandals: the complaints of the Spanish envoys in 171, who had to be heard by special panels (recuperatores) of senators, and the failure of the special court proposed against Servius Sulpicius Galba in 149 for his massacre of the Lusitanians. Previous cases had been handled through special commissions or popular trials, which were cumbersome and subject to political pressure. The new court gave a standing procedure for redress. Piso, later consul (133), censor and annalist, was known for his integrity (Frugi means 'honest').

The lex Calpurnia was the first of the permanent jury courts that would become the main forum of Roman political conflict in the late Republic. It was followed by the lex Junia (c. 126) and Gaius Gracchus' lex Acilia (123/122), which transferred the juries to the equestrians and made the procedure more effective, with a penalty of double restitution. Sulla and later Caesar reformed the extortion law. Cicero's prosecution of Verres in 70 is the most famous case. Modern historians (Lintott, Richardson) see the creation of the court as a sign of Senate concern over the conduct of governors and its effect on provincial loyalty, but also as a way of keeping the control of senatorial magistrates within the Senate itself. The court's effectiveness was limited: convictions were rare, since senators judged their peers.

scholarship: Lintott, The Leges de Repetundis and Associate Measures under the Republic, ZRG 98 (1981)
Richardson, The Purpose of the Lex Calpurnia de Repetundis, JRS 77 (1987)

set.detail:
Carthage lay on a peninsula connected to the mainland by an isthmus about 4.5 kilometres wide, defended by a triple line of walls: a ditch, a palisade, and a wall 13.5 metres high and 9 metres wide, with towers and two storeys housing 300 elephants, 4,000 horses and 20,000 infantry (Appian). The city, with a population of perhaps 200,000 to 400,000, had the Byrsa citadel and two harbours: a rectangular commercial harbour and a circular military harbour. After refusing to abandon the city, the Carthaginians armed themselves and called back Hasdrubal (the Boetharch), who commanded an army of 20,000 outside the city at Nepheris.

In 149 the consuls Manilius and Censorinus attacked the walls on the isthmus and on the narrow strip near the lagoon (the Lake of Tunis). Censorinus breached part of the wall with rams but the Carthaginians repaired it overnight and burned his engines. Manilius was beaten at Nepheris, where the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus saved part of the army. In 148 the consul Lucius Calpurnius Piso besieged other towns without success. In 147 the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul, though below the legal age, and gave him Africa without the usual lot. He restored discipline, took the suburb of Megara, built a siege wall across the isthmus to cut off supplies by land, and blocked the harbour entrance with a mole, while the Carthaginians cut a new channel to the sea.

In winter 147/146 Laelius and Gulussa destroyed the Carthaginian army at Nepheris. In spring 146, the Romans attacked the commercial harbour and fought their way through the streets towards the Byrsa, house by house, for six days. Appian's account (Punica 127-131), based on Polybius, an eyewitness, describes the horrors. The siege of Carthage, with Polybius present, is one of the best documented in antiquity. Excavations by the UNESCO campaign (1970s-1980s) have revealed traces of the destruction, including burnt houses on the Byrsa slopes and the circular harbour's shipsheds.

scholarship: Lancel, Carthage (1995)
Hurst, Excavations at Carthage: The British Mission II.1, The Circular Harbour, North Side (1994)
Le Bohec, Histoire militaire des guerres puniques (1996)

set.detail:
In spring 146, after taking the harbour area, Scipio Aemilianus' troops advanced through the streets towards the Byrsa, the citadel, along three streets lined with six-storey houses. Appian (Punica 128-131), following Polybius, describes the fighting from roof to roof, the burning of the houses, and the bodies of the dead and living thrown into pits and trampled by the cavalry. After six days, 50,000 men, women and children came down from the Byrsa and surrendered, and were sold as slaves. 900 Roman deserters, who could expect no mercy, held out in the temple of Eshmun with Hasdrubal and his family. Hasdrubal surrendered to Scipio; his wife, cursing him, threw herself and her children into the flames of the burning temple.

Polybius, who was at Scipio's side, describes how Scipio wept as he watched the city burn and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy (Iliad 6.448-449), saying that he feared the same fate would one day befall Rome. The city was plundered for days, and Scipio returned the art taken from Sicilian cities by the Carthaginians. The Senate sent ten commissioners who ordered the city to be razed completely; the site was cursed, and no one was to live there. The story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt is a modern invention (first attested in the 19th century).

The destruction of Carthage, the same year as that of Corinth, marked the end of the independent powers of the Mediterranean. Its territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica. Modern historians have discussed Rome's motives: fear of Carthaginian revival, Cato's campaign, Masinissa's ambitions, economic rivalry, or the ruthlessness of a hegemonic power. The ancient tradition, particularly Sallust, saw the destruction as a turning point in Roman morality: freed from fear of an external enemy (metus hostilis), the Roman elite fell into greed and internal strife. Gaius Gracchus attempted to found a colony (Junonia) on the site in 122; Caesar and Augustus refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, which became one of the largest cities of the empire.

scholarship: Ridley, To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage, CPh 81 (1986)
Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth (1995)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)

set.detail:
After the destruction of Carthage, the Senate's commissioners organised the former Carthaginian territory, about 25,000 square kilometres in the north-east of modern Tunisia, as the province of Africa. Its boundary with the Numidian kingdom was marked by a ditch, the fossa regia, which ran from the coast near Thabraca to Thaenae on the Lesser Syrtis; traces of it, with boundary stones restored under Vespasian, have been found. Utica, which had surrendered to Rome before the war, became the seat of the governor, a praetor or propraetor, and received the land between Carthage and Hippo Diarrhytus.

Seven towns that had supported Rome, including Utica, Hadrumetum, Leptis Minor, Thapsus, Acholla, Usalis and Theudalis, were declared free (civitates liberae et immunes). The other communities paid a fixed tribute (stipendium) and their land became Roman public land (ager publicus), partly leased to Roman and Italian settlers or to the indigenous people. The site of Carthage was cursed and abandoned. Masinissa's sons kept the territories that Numidia had taken from Carthage in previous decades.

The province was the first Roman possession in Africa and the beginning of a long process of Roman settlement and agricultural exploitation. The lex agraria of 111, preserved on a bronze tablet, regulated the status of land in Africa. Gaius Gracchus' attempt to found the colony of Junonia on the site of Carthage in 122 failed, but Marius settled veterans in the region, and Caesar and Augustus refounded Carthage as a colony and greatly expanded the province (Africa Proconsularis), which became one of the main sources of grain for Rome. Modern historians (Lintott, Raven) see the province's creation as the result of Rome's refusal to leave the territory to Numidia, which might have become too powerful, and the beginning of a Roman presence that lasted until the Vandal conquest of 439.

scholarship: Raven, Rome in Africa (1993)
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Di Vita-Évrard, La Fossa Regia, in L'Africa romana (1986)

set.detail:
After Critolaus' defeat at Scarpheia in Locris by Quintus Caecilius Metellus in 146, the Achaean League's last general, Diaeus, mobilised all available men, freed and armed 12,000 slaves, and imposed heavy levies on the cities. The consul Lucius Mummius, who had replaced Metellus, arrived at the Isthmus with 23,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry, reinforced by Cretan archers and Pergamene troops under Philopoemen (an Attalid officer), and camped near Corinth.

The Achaeans, encouraged by a minor success against the Roman outposts, attacked the Roman camp at Leucopetra on the Isthmus. According to Pausanias (7.16), the Achaean cavalry fled immediately when attacked by the Roman cavalry, and the Achaean infantry, after a short resistance, was taken in the flank by 1,000 Roman picked troops and routed. Diaeus fled to Megalopolis, killed his wife to prevent her from being captured, and committed suicide by poison. Many Achaeans took refuge in Corinth, but most fled the city at night.

Mummius waited three days before entering Corinth, fearing an ambush, then occupied the deserted city. The battle of Corinth (or Leucopetra) ended the Achaean War and the independence of the Achaean League. Pausanias is the main source, since the relevant books of Polybius and Livy are lost. Modern historians (Gruen, Kallet-Marx) emphasise the hopelessness of the Achaean position against Rome and the role of radical leaders in leading the League to war, although Polybius blamed them for madness. The battle marked the end of the last independent Greek power and is often regarded as the date of the end of Greek freedom. The destruction of Corinth that followed was ordered by the Senate as an example to Greece.

scholarship: Gruen, The Origins of the Achaean War, JHS 96 (1976)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

set.detail:
After the defeat of the Achaean army at Leucopetra, Lucius Mummius entered Corinth, which had been largely abandoned, killed the men who remained, sold the women and children into slavery, and, on the orders of the Senate, razed the city and burned it. Corinth, one of the richest and most famous cities of Greece, with its two harbours on the Isthmus (Lechaeum and Cenchreae), had been the site of the Isthmian proclamation of Greek freedom in 196 and the seat of Achaean League meetings, where Roman envoys had been insulted in 147.

Polybius, who arrived after the sack, saw Roman soldiers playing dice on famous paintings thrown on the ground, including Aristides' Dionysus. Mummius, a new man with no interest in Greek art, shipped huge quantities of statues and paintings to Rome and Italy, warning the contractors, according to Velleius, that if they lost any, they would have to replace them with new ones. Statues from Corinth were dedicated in Rome and in many Italian towns; inscriptions recording Mummius' gifts have been found at Italica in Spain, at Parma and elsewhere. Attalus II bought Aristides' painting for 600,000 sesterces, which made Mummius suspect it had value and withdraw it.

The destruction of Corinth, in the same year as Carthage, horrified the Greek world and became the symbol of Roman brutality. Its territory became Roman public land, part given to Sicyon. Excavations show that the site was not entirely deserted: some buildings, like the temple of Apollo, survived, and squatters occupied it until Caesar founded the Roman colony Laus Iulia Corinthiensis in 44, which became the capital of the province of Achaea. Modern historians (Purcell) have compared the two sacks of 146, seeing in them a deliberate demonstration of Roman power, while others note that the destruction of Corinth was less complete than the literary sources suggest.

scholarship: Purcell, On the Sacking of Carthage and Corinth (1995)
Williams and Bookidis (eds.), Corinth: The Centenary 1896-1996 (2003)

set.detail:
After the defeat of Andriscus by Quintus Caecilius Metellus in 148, Rome abandoned the system of four republics established in 167 and made Macedonia a permanent province, governed by a praetor or proconsul, with responsibility for the defence of the northern frontier against the Thracians, Dardanians and Scordisci. The governor also supervised Greek affairs, since Achaea was not organised as a separate province until 27. The precise date of the province's creation is debated; some put it in 148, others in 146 after the Achaean War, when the ten commissioners settled Greece.

The four merides continued to exist as administrative units with their own councils and coinage until the 1st century. A new era, the Macedonian provincial era, began in 148, used for dating inscriptions in the region. The Via Egnatia, built by the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius in the following years (probably between 146 and 120), linked Dyrrachium and Apollonia on the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica, the capital of the province, and later to Byzantium. Milestones with the name of Egnatius and the distance in Roman miles, found near Thessalonica, are among the earliest Roman milestones.

The province was the first permanent Roman possession in the Greek East, and the beginning of Roman territorial rule there. It was a frontier province, with constant wars against the Thracians and Scordisci; several governors were defeated or killed (for example, Gaius Porcius Cato in 114). Polybius had seen the Roman settlement of Greece as the end of his history. Modern historians (Kallet-Marx) emphasise that the province's creation marked a shift from indirect hegemony to direct rule, although Rome's control of Greece remained loose until the Mithridatic Wars. The Via Egnatia became one of the main roads of the empire, connecting Italy and the East, and was used by armies, merchants and later Christian missionaries, including Paul.

scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
Romiopoulou, Un nouveau milliaire de la via Egnatia, BCH 98 (1974)
Papazoglou, Les villes de Macédoine à l'époque romaine (1988)

set.detail:
In 139 the tribune Aulus Gabinius, grandson of a slave according to Cicero's hostile remark, carried a law introducing the secret written ballot (tabella) in the election of magistrates, replacing oral voting, in which each voter declared his choice to an official (rogator) who recorded it. Cicero (Laws 3.35) calls the lex Gabinia the first of the four ballot laws (leges tabellariae), followed by the lex Cassia (137) for popular trials except treason, the lex Papiria (131) for legislative assemblies, and the lex Coelia (107) for treason trials.

Under the new system, each voter received a small wooden tablet coated with wax, on which he wrote the initials of the candidates he chose, and dropped it into an urn (cista) as he crossed the narrow bridges (pontes) to the voting enclosures. Coins of the period, notably a denarius of Publius Licinius Nerva (c. 113), depict voters crossing the pons and receiving or depositing the tabella. The law was opposed by the aristocracy, who saw it as an attack on their influence over voters, especially their clients, who could no longer be observed and controlled.

Cicero, in On the Laws, has his brother Quintus attack the ballot laws for destroying the authority of the optimates, while Cicero defends a compromise in which the ballot is shown to the optimates. Modern historians debate the effect of the laws: some (Taylor, Yakobson) see them as increasing the independence of voters and the importance of popular politics; others (Gruen, Mouritsen) doubt their impact on elections, arguing that patronage and bribery continued. The lex Gabinia is also interpreted as a measure against bribery, since bribers could no longer verify that votes were delivered. It coincided with a period of political tension, with the Numantine War, the levy crises and the expulsion of Chaldaeans, preceding the Gracchan reforms.

scholarship: Yakobson, Secret Ballot and Its Effects in the Late Roman Republic, Hermes 123 (1995)
Taylor, Roman Voting Assemblies (1966)
Mouritsen, Plebs and Politics in the Late Roman Republic (2001)

set.detail:
Viriathus, a Lusitanian shepherd and survivor of Galba's massacre of 150, had led the Lusitanian resistance since 147, defeating a series of Roman commanders (Vetilius, Plautius, Unimanus, Nigidius) with guerrilla tactics and feigned retreats. In 140, after trapping the army of Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus at Erisane, he granted a peace treaty under which he was recognised as a friend of the Roman people and the Lusitanians kept their land; the treaty was ratified by the Roman people.

In 140/139 Servilianus' brother Quintus Servilius Caepio, consul for 140, obtained permission from the Senate to break the treaty secretly and then openly, and attacked Viriathus. Viriathus sent three of his friends, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, from the town of Urso, to negotiate with Caepio. Caepio bribed them with promises of great rewards to kill Viriathus. They returned to his camp and stabbed him in the throat while he slept in his armour. When they went to Caepio for their reward, he sent them to Rome, where the Senate refused to pay, saying 'Rome does not pay traitors' (a phrase attributed by later tradition).

Viriathus' followers gave him a magnificent funeral, burning his body on a great pyre with funeral games and gladiatorial combats around it. His successor Tautalus surrendered to Caepio soon after, and the Lusitanians were settled at Valentia (138) by Decimus Junius Brutus. Viriathus became a hero of the resistance against Rome; Diodorus (from Posidonius) praised his justice and frugality. In Portuguese national tradition he became a founding hero. Modern historians debate the nature of his leadership, some seeing him as a bandit chief, others as the leader of a social or national movement. The assassination, a clear violation of fides, was criticised by ancient writers (Velleius, Appian), and illustrates the brutality of the Roman wars in Spain. Caepio was refused a triumph.

scholarship: Pastor Muñoz, Viriato: la lucha por la libertad (2000)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

set.detail:
Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, consul in 137, took command of the war against Numantia, the Celtiberian town on the upper Douro that had defeated several Roman generals since 143. After several reverses, on hearing a false rumour that the Cantabri and Vaccaei were coming to help the Numantines, he abandoned his camp at night and withdrew to the site of Nobilior's old camp of 153. The Numantines, only 4,000 strong according to Appian, surrounded the Roman army of 20,000 and threatened to destroy it.

Mancinus negotiated a treaty with the Numantines through his quaestor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, whose father had made the moderate treaties of 179 and who was respected by the Celtiberians. The treaty, sworn by Mancinus and his officers, recognised Numantine independence and Roman friendship, in exchange for the release of the Roman army. The Numantines also returned Gracchus' account books, which they had taken from the camp. According to Plutarch, Gracchus saved 20,000 Roman citizens, besides slaves and camp followers.

In Rome, the Senate rejected the treaty as shameful, following the precedent of the Caudine Forks (321). To free Rome from its oath, it decreed in 136 that Mancinus be handed over to the Numantines, naked and bound; the Numantines refused to accept him, and he returned to Rome, where he set up a statue of himself in chains. Gracchus, whose treaty was repudiated, became embittered towards the Senate, according to Plutarch, a factor in his later tribunate. The episode raised profound questions about Roman fides and the rights of commanders to make treaties, and was debated by lawyers like Publius Mucius Scaevola (Cicero, On Duties 3.109). Modern historians see it as a symptom of the crisis of the Roman army in Spain and of the political tensions that preceded the Gracchan era. Scipio Aemilianus took command in 134 to finish the war.

scholarship: Rosenstein, Imperatores Victi (1990)
Rich, The Fetiales and Roman International Relations, in Priests and State (2011)

set.detail:
In 135 (or 136, or as early as 138), slaves on the estates of Sicily revolted. Diodorus (34/35.2), following Posidonius, explains the causes: after the Second Punic War, wealthy Sicilians and Romans bought large numbers of slaves, many of them recently enslaved from the eastern wars, to work on large estates and as herdsmen; they treated them harshly, branding them, underfeeding and overworking them; herdsmen were allowed to rob travellers to feed themselves. The revolt began at Enna, where the slaves of the cruel master Damophilus, led by Eunus, a Syrian slave from Apamea who claimed to have visions and could breathe fire (by hiding a nutshell of fire in his mouth), seized the city and killed Damophilus and his wife Megallis, sparing their daughter, who had been kind to them.

Eunus took the name Antiochus and the royal title, set up a court and a council, and minted coins with the image of Demeter and the legend 'King Antiochus'. Another revolt broke out in the south-west under Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, who joined Eunus. The rebels, said to number 70,000 to 200,000, defeated several Roman praetors and controlled much of the island, including Tauromenium and Enna. The Roman state was slow to respond, preoccupied with Numantia. Similar revolts broke out at Minturnae, Sinuessa, Delos and Attica, inspired by the Sicilian example.

The war was ended in 132 by the consul Publius Rupilius, who besieged and captured Tauromenium and Enna; Eunus was captured and died in prison at Morgantina, and Rupilius issued a law (lex Rupilia) for the administration of Sicily. The First Servile War was the largest slave revolt in antiquity before Spartacus. Modern historians (Bradley, Shaw) see it as a consequence of the development of the slave economy in the second century, and debate whether the revolt aimed to overthrow slavery or to establish a Hellenistic-style kingdom. It formed part of the background of social crisis that Tiberius Gracchus addressed in 133.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Urbainczyk, Slave Revolts in Antiquity (2008)

set.detail:
After a decade of Roman defeats at Numantia, the people elected Scipio Aemilianus consul for 134, setting aside the law banning second consulships, and gave him command in Spain. The Senate gave him no new legions, so he brought 4,000 volunteers, including friends and clients, and a cohort of 500 friends (cohors amicorum) including the historian Polybius, the young Gaius Marius, the future king Jugurtha, and the poet Lucilius. He found the army demoralised and spent months restoring discipline, expelling 2,000 prostitutes, traders and diviners, selling the soldiers' wagons, and training the men with marches and the construction of camps.

In summer 134 Scipio ravaged the lands of the Vaccaei to cut off Numantia's supplies, then surrounded the city, which sat on a hill at the confluence of the Douro and Merdancho, with a circuit of fortifications about nine kilometres long, with seven camps, towers, a wall 3 metres wide and 2.4 metres high, and a boom across the Douro. He had 60,000 men against perhaps 8,000 Numantines. The Numantines attempted sorties and sent the hero Retogenes Caraunius to seek help from other Celtiberian towns; the young men of Lutia agreed, but Scipio marched there and cut off the hands of 400 of them.

After eight months of famine, in which the inhabitants were reduced to cannibalism, Numantia surrendered in summer 133. Many inhabitants killed themselves; the survivors were sold, except 50 kept for Scipio's triumph, and the town was razed. Scipio took the cognomen Numantinus. Schulten's excavations (1905-1912) identified Scipio's camps and siege works, such as Castillejo and Peña Redonda, among the best preserved Roman siege works of the Republic; Schulten's interpretations have since been revised, and recent research has re-examined the circumvallation. The fall of Numantia ended the Celtiberian wars and is a symbol of resistance in Spanish national history. Appian's account (Iberica 84-98) comes from Polybius' lost monograph on the Numantine War.

scholarship: Schulten, Numantia I-IV (1914-1931)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)
